projectOutComesReport:
One frontier of plasma science focuses high-power lasers onto millimeter-sized frozen nuclear fuel pellets to generate fusion energy. The lasers create a plasma that heats the fuel target to millions of degrees under extremely high pressure. This violent heating and compression happens in less than a billionth of a second.

To get the most energy out of the fuel, scientists create advanced computer models to predict exactly how and when the energy is produced. The mathematical equations that go into the models are extremely difficult to solve, so scientists use simplified equations to approximate how the laser energy is absorbed, how the plasma is generated, how the plasma heats and compresses the fuel, how the fusion energy is distributed throughout the reacting fuel, and how that energy finally gets out. The simplified equations still need to accurately describe collisions, thermalization, and equilibration. They must accurately describe how electric, magnetic, and radiation fields develop and evolve as the plasma ions and electrons interact, and how the atoms in the fuel mix together and also mix with the fusion energy products. It is challenging to find an accurate description of these processes as the fuel heats up from a frozen pellet to a plasma as hot as the Sun, so the computer models need to be verified.

Our experiment is perfectly designed to test parts of these plasma physics models. We make a low temperature, low density plasma and measure how the ions interact. We are specifically interested in how particles and energy are transported through the plasma when (1) the plasma starts far from equilibrium and (2) when magnetic fields are present. Using precision laser spectroscopy, we measure how the ion density and temperature change with time.

Even though our experiments occur at low temperatures and densities, we can make direct comparisons to the fusion-class experiments using a clever mathematical trick. Plasmas can be characterized by a ratio of energies. A parameter called the “Coulomb strong-coupling parameter” is obtained by dividing the nearest-neighbor interaction energy by the average kinetic energy of the particles in the plasma. This ratio scales as the cube-root of density divided by the temperature. When we use this mathematical trick, our plasmas have the same strong-coupling parameter as the laser-driven fusion experiments.

For this grant, we made the following contributions to high-energy-density plasma science.

  1. We studied binary mixtures of ions, comparing our measurements to state-of-the-art molecular dynamics simulations. We found that the time- and velocity-integrated cross-sections used in many computer models fail to correctly predict the rate at which hot and cold ions come into equilibrium.
  2. We measured the rate at which ions carry energy across magnetic field lines, showing that the popular diffusion model does not accurately predict this process in our work.
  3. For partially magnetized plasmas, we discovered transient modes whose appearance and evolution cannot be predicted using standard plasma theories.
  4. We measured plasma expansion and confinement in a magnetic cusp field.
  5. We developed a new method for measuring the six-dimensional ion distribution function in our ultracold plasmas. Working with scientists at Los Alamos National Lab, we compared our results to predictions from high fidelity kinetic codes.

We published 8 peer-reviewed papers. My students and collaborators and I presented 11 conference papers directly related to this grant. In addition, my collaborators and I gave five invited presentations at national laboratories, universities, and international workshops.

abstractText:
Social media data can provide important clues and local knowledge that can help emergency managers and responders better comprehend and capture the evolving nature of many disasters. Yet humans alone cannot grasp the vast data generated by social media, so computers are used to assist.  Very little is currently known about how to leverage the skills of humans and machines when they work together (human-machine teaming) to identify meaningful patterns in social media data.  Therefore, the fundamental issues this Rapid Response Research (RAPID) project seeks to address are 1) understanding the process of real-time decisions that human digital volunteers make when they rapidly convert social media data into structured codes the machine (Artificial Intelligence algorithms) can understand, and 2) using this knowledge to improve human-machine teaming.  This project advances the field by revealing the unique abilities that both humans and machines bring when working together to comprehend social media patterns during an evolving disaster.  It supports education and diversity by providing research experiences to diverse students, as well as generating data useful for interdisciplinary courses teaching teamwork, social media analysis, and human-machine teaming. Finally, the findings can help emergency managers better train their volunteers who comb through social media using their understanding of the local knowledge and built environment to help machines see new patterns in data.  Hence, this project supports NSF's mission to promote the progress of science and to advance the nation's health, prosperity, and welfare by articulating the unique value that both humans and computers bring that can lead to better decisions during disasters.  The goal of this research is to better understand the real-time decisions that human annotators make under different environmental constraints, and how those contribute to the learning of Artificial Intelligence (AI) models. Under time constraints and information overload, human decision-making capabilities are limited; yet, humans still have a unique ability to understand the contextual references to the structures in the built environment that machines cannot recognize. For example, the meaning of the tweet, “Memorial is overloaded,” -- which means the hospital, called Memorial, is out of beds for patients —- can be lost on AI systems that lack the knowledge of the built environment. This example demonstrates the value that humans in the loop offer in a human-AI teaming context.  

This research focuses on capturing the ephemeral data from a variety of social media sources and our two research thrusts include: 1) online observations of Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) volunteers and a manager (a collaborator on this project) using think-aloud and cognitive interviewing strategies to reveal the real-time mental models used to make coding decisions for annotation tasks; and 2) an empirical analysis of different sampling algorithms for active (machine) learning paradigms to develop a typology of machine errors under diverse contexts that affect the quality of human decision making for annotation. This research will generate design guidelines that bridge the gap between the mechanisms used for real-time data processing with AI models and the understanding of context contributed by a human user teaming with the AI models.  Using theories of human decision-making combined with knowledge of how AI functions, this project provides a real-time, mid-disaster examination of 1) how humans understand, process, and interpret social media messages, and 2) how to refine AI algorithms to optimize active learning paradigm. This understanding will provide a theoretical framework enabling future research to develop protocols to optimize human-AI teaming by using concepts such as motivation and information theory. This work can help emergency managers conduct better training of their CERT volunteers and other annotators and provide clearer guidelines for how to communicate the unique value that humans bring to the annotation process for AI systems. Both our protocols and developed understanding of how humans interact with AI systems will be helpful for global health organizations, local and state-level disaster decision-makers, as well as provide direction for the vast CERT network in the United States.

projectOutComesReport:
RAPID: Collaborative Research: Human-AI Teaming for Big Data Analytics to Enhance Response to the COVID-19 Pandemic                 NSF Award #2029692

Keri K. Stephens, Moody College of Communication at The University of Texas at Austin, Amanda L. Hughes, Information Technology & Cybersecurity, at Brigham Young University, Hemant Purohit, Information Science & Technology at George Mason University. 

Social media data can provide important clues and local knowledge that can help emergency managers and responders better comprehend and capture the evolving nature of many disasters. Yet humans alone cannot grasp the vast data generated by social media, so computers are used to assist. Very little is currently known about how to leverage the skills of humans and machines when they work together (human-machine teaming) to identify meaningful patterns in social media data. Therefore, the fundamental issues this Rapid Response Research (RAPID) project seeks to address are 1) understanding the process of real-time decisions that human digital volunteers make when they rapidly convert social media data into structured codes the machine (Artificial Intelligence algorithms) can understand, and 2) using this knowledge to improve human-machine teaming. This project advances the field by revealing the unique abilities that both humans and machines bring when working together to comprehend social media patterns during an evolving disaster. It supports education and diversity by providing research experiences to diverse students, as well as generating data useful for interdisciplinary courses teaching teamwork, social media analysis, and human-machine teaming. Finally, the findings can help emergency managers better train their volunteers who comb through social media using their understanding of the local knowledge and built environment to help machines see new patterns in data. Hence, this project supports NSF's mission to promote the progress of science and to advance the nation's health, prosperity, and welfare by articulating the unique value that both humans and computers bring that can lead to better decisions during disasters. The goal of this research is to better understand the real-time decisions that human annotators make under different environmental constraints, and how those contribute to the learning of Artificial Intelligence (AI) models. Under time constraints and information overload, human decision-making capabilities are limited; yet, humans still have a unique ability to understand the contextual references to the structures in the built environment that machines cannot recognize. For example, the meaning of the tweet, ?Memorial is overloaded,? ?which means the hospital, called Memorial, is out of beds for patients?can be lost on AI systems that lack the knowledge of the built environment. This example demonstrates the value that humans in the loop offer in a human-AI teaming context.

This research focuses on capturing the ephemeral data from a variety of social media sources and our two research thrusts include: 1) online observations of Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) volunteers and a manager (a collaborator on this project) using think-aloud and cognitive interviewing strategies to reveal the real-time mental models used to make coding decisions for annotation tasks; and 2) an empirical analysis of different sampling algorithms for active (machine) learning paradigms to develop a typology of machine errors under diverse contexts that affect the quality of human decision making for annotation. This research will generate design guidelines that bridge the gap between the mechanisms used for real-time data processing with AI models and the understanding of context contributed by a human user teaming with the AI models. Using theories of human decision-making combined with knowledge of how AI functions, this project provides a real-time, mid-disaster examination of 1) how humans understand, process, and interpret social media messages, and 2) how to refine AI algorithms to optimize active learning paradigm. This understanding will provide a theoretical framework enabling future research to develop protocols to optimize human-AI teaming by using concepts such as motivation and information theory. This work can help emergency managers conduct better training of their CERT volunteers and other annotators and provide clearer guidelines for how to communicate the unique value that humans bring to the annotation process for AI systems. Both our protocols and developed understanding of how humans interact with AI systems will be helpful for global health organizations, local and state-level disaster decision-makers, as well as provide direction for the vast CERT network in the United States.

abstractText:
One major impediment in the wind energy field is managing the power losses (10-30%) that occur in a wind farm because of wake interference.  Mitigating these losses by even a few percent would have a major impact on our ability to abundantly produce clean energy and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Reducing these losses requires untangling the complexities of wind farm flow behavior.  Wind farms typically consist of 10s or 100s of turbines, with rotating blades creating wakes that mix and interact, affected by terrain and atmospheric behavior across many scales.  Vortex particle methods have been demonstrated to be an effective approach for simulating wake-dominant flows in adjacent fields (e.g., rotorcraft) and can potentially offer insight into wind farm flow fields at much faster computational speeds compared to traditional methods.  However, efficiently propagating vortex particles around viscous walls (e.g., terrain, other turbines) remains a challenge that is a focal point of this proposal.  The fundamental methodology could potentially be useful in other wake-dominant flow fields like simulating aircraft, underwater vehicles, the motion of water or smoke around other objects, etc. The project will also facilitate the development of a learn-by-doing platform to introduce students to computational aerodynamics—like a Codecademy® for aerodynamics.

The viscous vortex particle method is based on solving the vorticity form of the Navier-Stokes equations, and, using a meshless Lagrangian scheme, which can accurately preserve vortical structures and improve computational efficiency by placing particles only where needed. The first objective is to extend the methodology to allow for efficient propagation of particles around viscous walls.  The second objective is to leverage the speed of the proposed methodology to create a new analytical wake model appropriate for mixed height wind farms. Recent work has demonstrated that mixed height wind farms have the potential for a significant increase in power production.  Existing analytical wake models are often not appropriate for these scenarios as they do not include important coupling effects such as mixing and entrainment.  So, the third objective is to conduct broad sensitivity studies to identify the most relevant parameters and strategies to mitigate the negative effects of partial waking. Wind turbines often encounter incoming wakes over just a portion of the rotor disk causing asymmetric loading and potentially increased fatigue damage and noise. The proposed methodology provides a good balance between capturing the fidelity in flow physics with prediction speed to enable a robust exploration of wake interactions.

projectOutComesReport:
Early in this project we found that vortex particle methods (VPM) suffer from numerical stability and pivoted our efforts.  We were able to derive a new set of governing equations from the LES-filtered Navier-Stokes equations.  These new equations satisfy conservation of angular momentum (whereas existing VPM theory does not).  We refer to these new equations as the reformulated vortex particle method. With the increased stability, simulations could run longer, and so we then needed to address the turbulent energy cascade with a subgrid scale model (we refer to the subgrid scale model as a subfilter model since the methodology is meshless).  We developed a new anisotropic dynamic model of subfilter-scale vortex stretching.  Validations were performed of a turbulent round jet and an aircraft rotor in hover (and supplementary validations of leapfrogging vortex rings).  This work was published in an open-access paper: https://arc.aiaa.org/doi/epdf/10.2514/1.J063045  The code was open-sourced at: https://github.com/byuflowlab/FLOWVPM.jl

Next, we extended the methodology with actuator line methods, and a novel vorticity-based actuator surface method to enable broader interactional aerodynamic studies. There were some excellent published experimental datasets for wing-mounted propellers so we focused on these for additional validation studiers.  We performed several validations of the loads and flow field for propeller-wing interactions of a tailplane with tip-mounted propellers and a blown wing with mid-span-mounted propellers.  The postprint of this paper (10.2514/1.C037279) is available in an institutional repository: https://scholarsarchive.byu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=7695&context=facpub 

An open-source code framework for all of these methodologies, called FLOWUnsteady, is available at: https://github.com/byuflowlab/FLOWUnsteady with extensive documentation at: https://flow.byu.edu/FLOWUnsteady/ The documentation includes 8 detailed tutorials, theory, api descriptions, visualization guides, and many demonstration videos.  The code is written in Julia.

Ongoing work is extending the methodology to efficiently incorporate (inviscid) solid boundaries through a generalized fast multipole method. 

Educational efforts focused on creating a freely available textbook that focused on numerical implementation of various aerodynamic methods in a learn-by-doing manner.  While covering fundamental aerodynamic theory the text describes a 2d panel method, integral boundary layer method, vortex lattice method, blade element momentum method, and corrections to potential flow theory for compressible flow.  The text and problems are often used as onboarding problems for new students in our research lab. This is an ongoing work but is available at: http://flowlab.groups.et.byu.net/me515/aero.pdf  A set of youtube videos for some of these topics was also created at: https://youtube.com/playlist?list=PLj6pNSgoumydi4tiofayriGGjK-XiEsUY

abstractText:
This conference aims to contribute to increased quality of college mathematics teaching and learning.  It will do so by addressing how to generate, store, and share knowledge about effective college mathematics teaching. Participants will discuss the practical and theoretical issues about building a knowledge based for teaching college mathematics. During the conference, approximately 20 participants will begin to develop a formal system for generating, storing, and sharing knowledge of college mathematics instruction. Before the conference, the participants chosen will begin drafting written instructional products and use them at the conference to share instructional knowledge. 

A main goal of the conference is to elaborate a framework for potential authors of written instructional products to describe what knowledge they should capture and what type of scholarly work can be done to generate such knowledge. The conference includes a draft framework, called “Scholarly Design,” which is based on research and scholarship of teaching and learning. The major goal of the conference is to produce a framework characterizing Design Scholarship in mathematics, illustrated with specific examples of such scholarship.  It is anticipated that this framework will help faculty begin to engage in building a knowledge base for teaching in more effective ways.  Two additional benefits are expected to emerge from supporting this community of college mathematics teachers as they engage in Design Scholarship to build a knowledge base for teaching. First, college mathematics teachers may consume the published products, adapt them for their students and instructional contexts, and implement high quality lessons. Second, teachers who engage in the process of Design Scholarship will learn about teaching (or how to analyze teaching) that may apply to other mathematics lessons, not just the lesson that is the focus of their work.

projectOutComesReport:
In the Summer of 2020, the PI and Co-PI held an NSF funded workshop/conference titled, Building a Knowledge Base for Teaching Undergraduate Mathematics. They invited 18 mathematicians and mathematics educators from around the US to participate in this workshop. Due to Covid-19 restrictions the workshops were held online over 3 weeks rather than in-person over a 3-days. The goals of the workshop were:  

(a) Understanding the current knowledge base of teaching in undergraduate mathematics; (b) Developing a written genre that can be used to store and share important knowledge of teaching that is not widely available; (c) Write up examples of this genre and use them to better understand what features are needed/useful to best share important knowledge of teaching; d) Create a book that explains the work done at the conference and offers multiple high-quality examples of this written genre.

The workshop included four, two-hour sessions with all members present, and 3 session in small groups to discuss the details of a participants draft in this new genre (what we came to call a Lesson Analysis Manuscript, or LAM). The sessions were very productive. The first two were largely about building a consensus about what kind of knowledge is needed and how this genre relates to other available instructional materials (such as inquiry-oriented curriculum materials). The small group sessions were instrumental in testing out and discussion specific attempts and sharing individual visions of what the genre could contain and be. The latter sessions were helpful in refining/framing the content of the LAMs and to solidify a structure for the write-ups.

After the workshop sessions, we worked asynchronously in small groups to write a “how to” chapter to serve as a guide for us, as well as others, on how to write LAMs. We then used the ideas from that chapter to refine our individual chapters (19 of the 20 participants were invited to write a LAM, with the current MAA president the one participant who we did not expect to write up a LAM due to his heavy load as president). After completion of the “how to” chapter, participants revised their chapters/LAMs to meet the expectations in the chapters. Drafts were due by the first of September, 2020. The PI and Co-PI read through each one and offered feedback. 12 of the chapters were selected for publication in the book (with some participants not able to submit a full, revised draft due time constraints, particularly increased time constraints due to preparing for online/blended instruction due to the Covid-19 restrictions).

Currently, the PI and Co-PI are making final edits on the manuscript of the book from the conference. MAA has agreed, in principle, to publish the book and we will be sending a complete manuscript to them in a few short weeks for them to review.

Surveys of the conference participants showed that they thought the problem that the conference addressed was important and the work we started is promising. Many of the participants have committed to be actively engaged in future efforts to share the work and build on what was started in this conference. Four journals have agreed that the LAM genre is a good fit and will accept LAMs submitted for publication.

The PI and Co-PI are planning on writing another NSF grant to hold another conference that will take up the issue of how to do the work of Lesson Analysis which we introduce in the book. The current book focuses on the written genre, but does not adequately help readers know how to do the work of studying teaching, and learning from practice, that would result in a LAM.   

Instructional knowledge is being developed by individuals, or in groups in a particular local context, but the community of college mathematics instructors does not have a field of scholarship that allows this knowledge to be vetted, shared, and stored; nor does the community have a clear idea of how to support others to learn from their own teaching practice in a way that can contribute to a broader knowledge base. We feel like we have made significant strides in this area and will continue to work on developing ideas about, and resources for, sharing instructional knowledge in college mathematics teaching.

abstractText:
With this award, the Chemical Measurements and Imaging Program of the Chemistry Division is funding Dr. James Harper of the University of Central Florida to extend the capability of theoretical methods to accurately predict crystal structures.  Presently, many compounds and even entire classes of compounds are unsuitable for analysis by conventional crystallography methods.  This project combines lattice prediction methods with experimental NMR data to provide new methodology capable of solving structural problems that are now intractable.  This outcome will impact society by improving the ability to characterize a host of new materials.  For example, nearly 60 cephalosporin antibiotics have been described since 1955, yet over 93% in the structures have never been characterized crystallographically. The project focuses on characterizing key cephalosporins as well as other challenging materials.

This project focuses on improving the theoretical prediction of crystal structure by including experimental solid-state NMR data in the prediction process.  The NMR data serve to identify a single high-probability conformation before the prediction process.  Because many lattice prediction programs robustly and accurately treat rigid structures but are challenged by flexibility, the NMR data improves prediction by limiting the conformational space searched.  The experimental NMR measurements focus primarily on 13C and 15N chemical shift tensors because such data provide three measurable parameters for each molecular position.  Uncertainties in atomic positions are provided through a molecular dynamics process, to ultimately create structures suitable for deposit into crystallographic databases.  The broader impact of this work includes training students from a primarily undergraduate institution (Washington and Jefferson College) in an annual three week NMR course involving 6-8 students, the creation of a series of Open Courseware lectures describing basic NMR concepts and the more specialized tensor measurement methods, and outreach into the scouting community of central Florida through lab tours and voluntary teaching of merit badge courses.

projectOutComesReport:
Work from this award resulted in 20 publications in peer-reviewed journals.  These publications have included 17 graduate students and 8 undergraduates as authors. Two of the students supported by this grant have now graduated with a Ph.D. and a third is expected to graduate in 2022. Broader impacts include teaching of a short course on NMR spectroscopy at two primarily undergraduate institutions and creating a chemistry related workshop for girl scouts.  More details on key outcomes are summarized below.

 

Publications - Intellectual outcomes. Key publications resulting from this funding are summarized below.

1.     Title: Predicting anisotropic thermal displacements for hydrogens from solid-state NMR: a study on hydrogen bonding in polymorphs of palmitic acid

Authors: Wang, L.; Uribe-Romo, F. J.; Mueller, L. J.; Harper, J. K.

Journal: Physical Chemistry Chemical Physics, 2018, Vol. 20, p. 8475.

Summary: An approach is described for predicting the errors in atom positions for crystal structures derived from nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy.  The uncertainties predicted by this approach are nearly ten times smaller than those obtained from x-ray diffraction and approximately half the magnitude of the errors from neutron diffraction data.

2.     Title: TensorView: A software tool for displaying NMR tensors

Authors: Young, R. P.; Lewis, C. R.; Yang, C.; Wang, L.; Harper, J. K.; Mueller, L.

Journal: Magnetic Resonance in Chemistry, 2018, Vol. 57, p. 211.

Summary: A software program is reported that allows the errors in atom positions to be displayed.  These NMR derived ellipsoids can be displayed on the atoms within a microcrystalline structure, even in cases where the crystal structure is unknown or a solid has only weak long range order.  An illustration where only the COOH hydrogen in a fatty acid was characterized in shown in Figure 1.

3.     Title: Monitoring the refinement of crystal structures with 15N solid-state NMR shift tensor data.

Authors: Kalakewich, K.; Iuliucci, R.; Mueller, K. T.; Eloranta, H.; Harper, J. K.

Journal: Journal of Chemical Physics, 2015, Vol. 143, article number 194702.

Summary: An improved NMR experiment is described for measuring N-15 chemical shift tensors and shown to be highly accurate.  A total of 39 values were measured spanning a range of nearly 400 ppm.  These data have become important benchmark data for several theoretical studies.  This study also includes work demonstrating one of the first accurate predictions of N-15 shift tensors using theoretical computational methods.

4.     Title: Exploiting 13C/14N solid-state distance measurements to assign dihedral angles and locate neighboring molecules.

Authors: Pope, G. M.; Hung, I.; Gan, Z.; Mobarak, H.; Widmalm, G.; Harper, J. K.

Journal: Chemical Communications, 2018, Vol. 54, p. 6376.

Summary: The NMR measurement of Carbon to nitrogen distances for multiple sites within a molecule was demonstrated. This study fulfills a long-standing expectation that C/N distance measurements will become an important tool in structural analysis of solids.  This work is the first to demonstrate that such structural information can now be obtained.  This study will be a valuable addition to structural studies of materials where the growth of crystals suitable for more conventional crystallography is difficult.

5.     Title: refining crystal structures using 13C NMR chemical shift tensors as a target function.

Authors: Wang, L.; Harper, J. K.

Journal: CrystEngComm, 2021,DOI: 10.1039/d1ce00960e.

Summary: This study demonstrates an NMR based refinement process that adjusts crystal structures from any source to create highly accurate final coordinates.  Several non-NMR metrics, examine before and after refinement, indicate that this process does not introduce structural errors. This refinement process appears to provide the most accurate computed 13C chemical shift data presently available.  An illustration of the agreement between computed and experimental shifts is shown in Figure 2.

 

Broader outcomes. Some of the important achievements are described below.

1.     A graduate level course on NMR spectroscopy (CHM 5937) was developed and taught at the University of Central Florida.

2.     A short-course was developed to teach basic principles of NMR at primarily undergraduate institutions.  Instruction was given at Washington and Jefferson College and Utah Valley University. Approximately 50 students have participated in the program.

3.     Community instruction.  During the funding period, mosquito borne infections from the Zika virus become a concern in Florida.  A workshop was developed aimed at educating girl scouts on the dangers of the Zika virus. This session allowed all participants to make a liter of mosquito repellent based on aloe vera and naturally occurring compounds.  This hour-long course has been in great demand over the past several years and over 100 girl scout and their leaders have participated.
